items.q: Do adjectives always keep the same form?
items.correct: No — they usually agree with the noun's gender and number.
items.why: In Spanish, French and German adjectives change endings to agree with the noun.

items.correct: No — word order and idioms differ, so literal translation often fails.
items.misconception: Yes, you can always translate one word at a time.
items.random_wrong: Languages share identical grammar to English.
items.why: 'False friends' and different sentence structures mean literal translation can mislead.

items.q: Do verbs have just one form?
items.correct: No — verbs conjugate to match the subject and the tense.
items.misconception: Yes, a verb only ever has one form.
items.random_wrong: Tense doesn't exist in other languages.
items.why: Verb endings change with who is doing the action and when (past, present, future).

items.q: Are accents and special characters optional decoration?
items.correct: No — they can change meaning or pronunciation and are part of correct spelling.
items.why: An accent or character (é, ñ, ß, ü) can change a word's sound or meaning entirely.
